analysis.one_liner: Restricts presidential pardons, emoluments, and emergency powers, speeds enforcement of congressional subpoenas, and tightens campaign-finance and election rules.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 220-208, with all but one Republican opposed, and the Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill was a package of checks on presidential power: it would have banned presidents from pardoning themselves, required presidential candidates to disclose ten years of tax returns, enforced the Constitution's bans on presidents taking gifts or payments from foreign and state governments, and given Congress faster tools to enforce its subpoenas. It also required campaigns to report foreign contacts, cracked down on deepfake election ads, paid for states to move to ranked-choice voting, strengthened whistleblower protections, and required cause to fire inspectors general. The House passed it in December 2021, but the Senate never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters benefit from a government where officials cannot self-pardon, accept payments from foreign or state governments through their businesses, or conceal their finances before running for president; from a Congress that can compel testimony and documents; and from stronger protections for the civil servants and whistleblowers who expose misconduct. Future officeholders of both parties would be bound by the same rules.

how_it_helps.text: It makes it easier for Congress to enforce subpoenas in court, which affects how readily officials must answer to oversight of agencies and spending.

It requires candidates for president and vice president to turn over 10 years of tax returns to the Federal Election Commission, giving the public visibility into a candidate's finances before election.
It bans presidential self-pardons and requires disclosure of materials behind pardons of people connected to the president.
It strengthens protections for whistleblowers and requires cause for removing inspectors general, the officials who investigate waste and misconduct inside agencies.
It bars campaigns from paying a candidate's spouse and tightens disclosure of inaugural committee donations, aimed at family and ally enrichment from campaign and inaugural funds.

analysis.who_pays: The president, vice president, and other executive officials lose some legal protections and discretion, and political campaigns and inaugural committees face new reporting and prohibition rules. Some administration powers to withhold information or redirect funds would be curtailed.

drawbacks.text: Penalties for subpoena noncompliance can fall personally on agency heads and authorize deduction of their legal fees from their salaries, which critics view as turning routine legal positions into personal financial risk and as an incentive for politically motivated litigation.

The bill binds the executive branch with new mandates (communications logs, apportionment publishing, foreign-contact reporting) that add compliance burdens and could chill candid advice within agencies.

Some provisions, such as a program supporting states' transition to ranked choice voting and a deepfake ban, are contested on the merits and were attached to a package billed as government-accountability reform.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real but diffuse: stronger checks on presidential misconduct, easier congressional investigations, better whistleblower protection, and tax transparency. The costs are modest—some constraints on executive flexibility, a heavier legal and compliance burden on the executive branch, and a possible wave of subpoena litigation. The bill's weakness is breadth: bundling dozens of reforms invites both true objections (some provisions, like subpoena penalties and the RCV program, deserve standalone scrutiny) and wholesale rejection. As a package aimed at officeholders rather than the public, its core value is deterrence of future executive abuses, which history suggests will matter regardless of which party holds power.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it in December 2021, but the Senate left it sitting after receiving it, so it never became law when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced September 21, 2021 and referred to nine House committees, with Oversight and Reform taking the lead.
On December 9, 2021, the House rejected a Republican motion to recommit the bill to committee, 212-217.
Later that day the House passed the bill 220-208, with 219 of 221 voting Democrats in favor and only 1 of 213 voting Republicans supporting it.
The bill was received in the Senate on December 13, 2021; no further action is recorded before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
All 168 cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republicans sponsored or cosponsored the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The sitting executive branch—officeholders who might otherwise face subpoena enforcement, emoluments enforcement, and tax-return disclosure—benefited from the bill's failure, along with outside groups that benefit from foreign money loopholes and lax campaign rules.

sides.party_line_note: The House vote split almost entirely by party: 219 of 221 Democrats voted yes while only 1 of 213 Republicans did, and no Senate chamber action followed.

industries.industry: Incumbent presidents and senior executive-branch officials
industries.note: The bill would expose their tax returns, pardon decisions, emoluments, and subpoena noncompliance to enforceable penalties. No incumbent of either party would be exempt, though the provisions were framed around recent abuses.

industries.industry: Online platforms and digital political advertisers
industries.note: The Honest Ads provisions expand disclaimer and political-record requirements to online political advertising, and a ban on deceptive media adds a compliance risk for platforms.
New foreign-contact reporting, deepfake, and spouse-payroll rules add compliance obligations but operate within the existing campaign industry rather than changing its structure.

Expanded OGE/OSC enforcement, new ethics rules for legal expense funds, and more subpoena litigation would generate professional work, while the bill also bars registered lobbyists from contributing to officials' legal expense funds.
